questions.question: What is the key property of a good embedding?
options: It compresses text to a single number
Texts with similar meanings produce vectors that are close together
It works without any training data
questions.explanation: Embeddings map text into a vector space where semantic similarity becomes spatial proximity — nearby points mean similar things.

questions.question: Why must you use the same embedding model for indexing and querying?
options: Different models produce vectors in different coordinate systems, so similarity scores are meaningless
Switching models voids the vector database warranty
questions.explanation: Each model maps text into its own vector space. Mixing models means comparing positions in different coordinate systems — the distances tell you nothing.

questions.question: Why is embedding an entire 50-page document as one vector a bad idea?
options: It exceeds the model's token limit
It averages out the meaning of every section, so retrieval can't pinpoint the relevant part
It violates vector database schema rules
questions.explanation: A single vector for a long document blurs all its topics together. Chunk first, then embed each chunk so retrieval can surface the right section.

questions.question: A user searches 'who can sign off on a $50K purchase' but no policy uses those exact words. What makes embeddings find the right document?
options: The query and the matching policy land close together in vector space despite different wording
The embedding model has a built-in synonym dictionary
Embeddings fall back to keyword matching when no exact match exists
questions.explanation: Embeddings capture meaning, not keywords. The query about signing off on purchases and a policy about expenditure approval are semantically close even with zero word overlap.
